problem.context: Bubba's internal editors prepared rough cuts from footage, scripts, storyboards, voice-over files and production notes.
problem.friction: They repeatedly gathered those materials from separate tools and folders, then organized them manually clip by clip.
problem.consequence: Time spent preparing and reconciling inputs grew with every video, making larger batches difficult to manage and monitor.
problem.statement: How might we help Bubba's internal editors prepare and monitor large video batches without repeating the same manual setup across disconnected tools?

stages.title: Understand the work around the edit
stages.activity: I reviewed the existing internal editing workflow, the production inputs editors handled and the decisions they needed to revisit during each run.
stages.insight: The bottleneck was not one editing control. It was the repeated work of gathering, aligning and checking related source material before editing could begin.
stages.decision: Treat the editors' preparation workflow as one connected internal system rather than a collection of isolated tools.

stages.title: Define the repeated work behind every batch
stages.activity: I mapped where internal editors had to collect inputs, confirm readiness, monitor a run and inspect its outputs.
stages.insight: Automation would only reduce the burden if editors could still see input readiness, current progress and output status.
stages.decision: Define success as reducing repetitive setup without removing editor oversight.

stages.title: Organize the workflow around production states
stages.activity: I compared automating individual utilities, using a linear wizard and creating an internal workspace organized by library, setup, progress and results.
stages.insight: A shared internal workspace kept production context available while still giving each state a clear focus.
stages.decision: Use one interface with distinct states instead of sending editors between disconnected tools.

stages.title: Make automation inspectable
stages.activity: I designed the internal editor workspace for media handling, timeline preparation, live progress, sampled frames and export readiness.
stages.insight: Editors needed to understand what the automation was doing and inspect suggested material before it entered the edit.
stages.decision: Keep logs, progress, frame notes and outputs reviewable inside the same internal production tool.

stages.title: Validate through increasing production scope
stages.activity: The initial 10-video prototype was expanded inside Bubba's working internal production process.
stages.insight: The unified workflow continued to support editors as batch size and operational responsibility increased.
stages.decision: Keep the unified model and extend it for production-scale monitoring, review and export.

resolution.before: Internal editors gathered scattered production inputs and organized them manually clip by clip before each run.
resolution.response: One internal production workspace connected setup, automated preparation, monitoring, review and export.
resolution.after: Internal editors could prepare and inspect large batches without losing the source context behind each run.
resolution.evidence: The tool grew from a 10-video prototype to more than 300 videos per automated batch and was adopted for internal production use.
resolution.reflection: Automation earns trust when its state and outputs remain legible to the people responsible for the work.

problem.context: People who discover a one-time run through platforms such as Luma still need directions, live updates, group awareness and a way to ask for help during the activity.
problem.friction: The usual workaround is to exchange contact information or create a permanent group chat for people who may only meet once.
problem.consequence: A short event leaves participants with another inbox, an ongoing identity connection and no clear agreement about when shared messages or location context should disappear.
problem.statement: How might we give a temporary running group the coordination of a group chat without creating a permanent social obligation?

stages.title: Follow the group from event page to the run
stages.activity: We examined Luma-style event journeys, the coordination moments that happen after sign-up and the social cost of moving a temporary group into permanent communication tools.
stages.insight: An event page could bring people together, but it did not provide the live, safety-aware coordination they needed once the activity began.
stages.decision: Create a communication layer whose lifespan matches the event rather than the participants' broader social identities.

stages.title: Define the mismatch between the group and its channel
stages.activity: We separated what the group needed during the event—entry, recognition, coordination and support—from what conventional chat tools kept afterward.
stages.insight: Participants needed enough identity and location context to stay safe, but not a permanent account connection or open-ended inbox.
stages.decision: Use account-free entry and temporary names while keeping role, location, help and retention states explicit.

stages.title: Split one room into two decision views
stages.activity: We compared a shared group feed with role-specific Host and Runner experiences.
stages.insight: Runners need fast personal actions while the Host needs a crew-level view of readiness, distance and alerts.
stages.decision: Keep one room state but translate it into distinct Host and Runner interfaces.

stages.title: Prototype the difficult moments first
stages.activity: I built QR entry, live run views, lightweight signals, Help, Water, Rest, Give Up, chat, results and retention states.
stages.insight: Large, explicit actions are easier to interpret while moving than subtle notifications or free-form messages.
stages.decision: Make safety requests immediate and keep the room's ending as visible as its entry.

stages.title: Walk through both sides of the same run
stages.activity: The interactive prototype was exercised across Host and Runner states to check shared data, alerts and closure behavior.
stages.insight: The role split clarified decisions while preserving one understandable group state.
stages.decision: Retain the two-role architecture and carry its key flows into future field evaluation.

resolution.before: Groups formed through event platforms still had to exchange contact information or create permanent chats for short-lived coordination.
resolution.response: PACEPOP created a purpose-bound room with QR entry, temporary identity, role-specific views and explicit retention.
resolution.after: Hosts and runners could coordinate the activity, respond to safety moments and close the shared space without exchanging contact information.
resolution.evidence: A working two-person prototype covers account-free entry, live coordination, support interactions, results and room closure.
resolution.reflection: Ephemerality is not the absence of features; it is a deliberate interaction rule that must include safety and closure.

problem.context: Automotive reviewers needed to inspect one vehicle model together in Apple Vision Pro.
problem.friction: CloudXR, Omniverse and visionOS split review controls, text input and collaborator presence across incompatible spaces.
problem.consequence: A visually shared model still failed to support ordinary shared-review actions such as pointing, measuring and annotating.
problem.statement: How might we make a streamed vehicle model support a collaborative spatial review despite platform-level interaction constraints?

stages.title: Follow the reviewer's actions, not the platform demo
stages.activity: The team mapped the actions reviewers needed around the vehicle and compared them with what the streamed experience actually supported.
stages.insight: Screen-bound text, scripted actions, missing spatial input and detached controls interrupted the review conversation.
stages.decision: Evaluate the experience through review behaviors rather than visual fidelity alone.

stages.title: Expose the space-model conflict
stages.activity: We documented how CloudXR Full Immersive Space and native shared-presence behavior competed for the same visual field.
stages.insight: The desired streamed model and visible native collaborators could not coexist as originally planned.
stages.decision: Separate the problem into review interactions, scene control and presence experiments that could be tested independently.

stages.title: Explore workarounds at the system boundary
stages.activity: The team considered native windows, a local event bridge, tracked avatars, passthrough references and lightweight information panels.
stages.insight: No single workaround solved every constraint, but each could make one critical review behavior testable.
stages.decision: Use a modular set of native and local prototypes instead of hiding the platform conflict behind a static concept.

stages.title: Bring review actions back to the vehicle
stages.activity: We built spatial notes, a local part-control bridge and presence analogues; I led the toolbar and review-panel direction.
stages.insight: Review controls became easier to understand when they stayed near the model and preserved action history.
stages.decision: Organize annotation, measurement, inspection, participants and history as one in-session toolkit.

stages.title: Demonstrate what works and document what does not
stages.activity: The sprint team exercised the technical prototypes and presented the interaction evidence and platform directions to Honda R&D.
stages.insight: The prototypes clarified both feasible review behaviors and the infrastructure decisions still required.
stages.decision: Present working pieces and system boundaries together so future platform choices remain grounded in reviewer needs.

resolution.before: Reviewers could see the same streamed vehicle but could not complete a shared review naturally around it.
resolution.response: A modular spatial toolkit combined native notes, direct part control, presence experiments and in-session review controls.
resolution.after: The team could demonstrate concrete review interactions while making the platform conflicts and next decisions explicit.
resolution.evidence: Working interaction prototypes and future platform directions were demonstrated to Honda R&D.
resolution.reflection: In spatial computing, designing the system boundary is often inseparable from designing the interface.

problem.context: Clinicians in an assessment-training workflow reviewed wound imagery, DISH categories and proposed terminology.
problem.friction: The image, category, keyword decision and supporting rationale could become separated across steps.
problem.consequence: A reviewer could record an answer without preserving enough context for another person to understand or revisit it.
problem.statement: How might we keep wound evidence, terminology and reasoning connected throughout an assessment-training workflow?

stages.title: Understand the decision behind the label
stages.activity: The cross-functional team incorporated input from clinicians and industry researchers while reviewing the assessment sequence.
stages.insight: A category or keyword alone did not explain what evidence the reviewer was judging.
stages.decision: Keep the wound image, category, terminology and progress visible around each decision.

stages.title: Make every assessment explainable
stages.activity: We reframed the task from simple keyword confirmation to a traceable decision with supporting context.
stages.insight: The workflow needed to capture both classification and the reason for disagreement.
stages.decision: Design one explicit decision at a time and preserve its evidence for review.

stages.title: Move from confirmation to active classification
stages.activity: The team compared binary validation with direct primary and secondary keyword selection.
stages.insight: A yes-or-no answer could check a suggestion but could not capture the clinician's own terminology choice.
stages.decision: Pair the image with primary and optional secondary terms, then ask for rationale when needed.

stages.title: Connect classification, rationale and review
stages.activity: I designed guided training, keyword selection, disagreement feedback and completed-assessment review states.
stages.insight: The review view needed to reassemble the evidence and decisions that had been collected across the flow.
stages.decision: Bring image, DISH category, selected terms and supporting context into one traceable record.

stages.title: Review the workflow with clinical and industry context
stages.activity: The cross-functional team reviewed the prototype states against the assessment sequence and available domain input.
stages.insight: The connected record made the relationship between evidence, terminology and rationale more explicit.
stages.decision: Carry the traceable workflow forward as a design exploration without presenting it as a deployed clinical system.

resolution.before: Assessment evidence and terminology decisions were difficult to interpret when separated across steps.
resolution.response: The prototype connected guided classification, optional rationale and a complete review record.
resolution.after: Reviewers could revisit the image, category, terminology and supporting context as one decision trail.
resolution.evidence: The collaboration produced a clinician-facing assessment-training prototype; it was not clinically validated or deployed.
resolution.reflection: In high-context workflows, clarity comes from preserving the reason behind a decision, not only the selected value.

problem.context: A swim-education nonprofit needed one website to serve families, schools, volunteers, donors and partners.
problem.friction: Each audience arrived with a different question, but the mission and available actions had to remain coherent.
problem.consequence: A site organized around the nonprofit rather than its audiences could hide the next meaningful action.
problem.statement: How might we turn one nonprofit mission into clear, credible paths for several audiences?

stages.title: Identify why each audience arrives
stages.activity: I reviewed the mission, stakeholder needs and the questions different visitors bring to the site.
stages.insight: Families, schools, volunteers, donors and partners shared the mission but needed different evidence and actions.
stages.decision: Start with audience intent rather than an internal organization chart.

stages.title: Make the next step visible
stages.activity: I translated audience needs into a small set of journeys and content priorities.
stages.insight: The site needed to explain impact and provide a clear next action without fragmenting the story.
stages.decision: Use mission, programs, impact and participation as the primary information structure.

stages.title: Balance a global story with local action
stages.activity: The team explored ways to show reach, active locations, program proof and direct calls to action in one flow.
stages.insight: A visual overview could establish scale, but audience-specific routes still needed to remain immediate.
stages.decision: Pair the global impact story with clear program and participation paths.

stages.title: Build the real responsive experience
stages.activity: I led UX/UI design, front-end implementation and publishing across desktop and mobile breakpoints.
stages.insight: Content hierarchy had to survive smaller screens and real publishing constraints.
stages.decision: Prototype in the production environment and resolve design and delivery together.

stages.title: Review the published paths
stages.activity: The live site was reviewed across key audience routes and responsive layouts before launch.
stages.insight: The same mission could remain consistent while each audience received a distinct next step.
stages.decision: Publish the shared structure and continue using the live site as the source of truth.

resolution.before: Several audiences needed different information from one nonprofit website.
resolution.response: The site organized the mission around audience journeys, proof of impact and direct actions.
resolution.after: Visitors could understand the organization and move toward the path relevant to them on desktop or mobile.
resolution.evidence: The responsive website was published at swimuphill.org.
resolution.reflection: Information architecture becomes more useful when it begins with why people arrive rather than how an organization is structured.

problem.context: Hospital billing teams recover charges that are missed during care delivery while physicians hold the clinical context needed to confirm them.
problem.friction: The recovery process can require repeated investigation and communication across roles.
problem.consequence: Revenue is delayed while clinicians and administrators absorb additional coordination work.
problem.statement: How might we surface a likely missed charge as one clear, traceable decision without removing human validation?

stages.title: Map the recovery work across roles
stages.activity: The team examined the missed-charge workflow, the information available to physicians and the follow-up work handled by administrators.
stages.insight: The product needed to reduce coordination without asking either role to understand the other's full workflow.
stages.decision: Design one shared service with role-specific decisions and visibility.

stages.title: Keep a human validation point
stages.activity: We defined the intervention around a pending encounter, supporting context and one physician decision.
stages.insight: An autonomous billing action would be difficult to trust when clinical context remained ambiguous.
stages.decision: Let the agent detect and prepare the case, but keep confirmation with the physician.

stages.title: Connect detection, confirmation and follow-up
stages.activity: We explored separate alerts, an administrator queue and a two-sided workflow connected through interoperable health data.
stages.insight: A single alert did not solve the downstream need to track status and recovery.
stages.decision: Create a closed loop from detection to physician validation and administrator resolution.

stages.title: Give each role one focused surface
stages.activity: We designed a mobile confirmation flow for physicians and a traceable queue for billing administrators.
stages.insight: Role-specific interfaces reduced the amount of system detail each person had to interpret.
stages.decision: Show clinical context at the decision point and operational status in the administrator view.

stages.title: Pressure-test the service through a live pitch
stages.activity: The concept, workflow and interfaces were reviewed through USC and Techstars Startup Weekend judging.
stages.insight: The strongest story connected a concrete workflow problem to a bounded agent role and human accountability.
stages.decision: Present the opportunity as phased product development rather than claiming a completed hospital pilot.

resolution.before: Missed charges created investigative and coordination work across clinical and billing roles.
resolution.response: HAiLY connected agent-assisted detection to one physician decision and a traceable administrator workflow.
resolution.after: Each role received the context and action needed to move the same case forward.
resolution.evidence: The two-sided service concept received second place at USC and Techstars Startup Weekend.
resolution.reflection: Agentic products are more credible when autonomy is bounded by a clear human decision and visible handoff.

problem.context: A campus anaphylaxis response depends on recognition, medication access and bystander action under time pressure.
problem.friction: Awareness, device location and instructions can live in separate systems or remain unknown until an emergency.
problem.consequence: A usable medication product alone cannot ensure that a nearby person can find and act with it quickly.
problem.statement: How might we connect campus awareness, medication access and confident bystander action into one response system?

stages.title: Study the emergency as a campus journey
stages.activity: The team reviewed preparedness scenarios, access points and the information a bystander would need before and during an event.
stages.insight: The response began long before device use: people had to recognize the risk, know where help was and feel able to act.
stages.decision: Treat awareness, location and administration as one service journey.

stages.title: Reduce uncertainty at every handoff
stages.activity: We framed the core gaps around finding medication, understanding availability and following a simple action sequence.
stages.insight: A delay at any handoff weakened the whole response.
stages.decision: Design a system that keeps location, status and instructions explicit.

stages.title: Combine service, interface and package
stages.activity: The team explored a campus map, access stations, directional guidance, awareness material and one-handed package concepts.
stages.insight: No single touchpoint could carry the entire response.
stages.decision: Use a connected service ecosystem with consistent guidance across digital and physical moments.

stages.title: Make the nearest useful action visible
stages.activity: I contributed service, package and interface design, including nearby-device status, directions and an accessible physical package direction.
stages.insight: The interface and package needed to reduce decisions rather than add instructional depth during an emergency.
stages.decision: Prioritize nearest-location guidance and direct, one-handed action cues.

stages.title: Review the system as one sprint proposal
stages.activity: The integrated service was reviewed in the USC industry challenge sprint with ARS Pharma.
stages.insight: The proposal was strongest when each touchpoint reinforced the same response sequence.
stages.decision: Present the design as a connected preparedness proposal, not a deployed emergency service.

resolution.before: Campus response depended on disconnected awareness, access and action moments.
resolution.response: The proposal connected a location interface, access system, package and awareness language.
resolution.after: A bystander-facing journey could move from recognizing the need to finding and using the nearest available medication.
resolution.evidence: The integrated service, package and interface concept was delivered as an Industry Challenge Sprint proposal.
resolution.reflection: Emergency design is a chain: every handoff must reduce uncertainty for the next one to work.

problem.context: People without programming knowledge were exploring branching stories with generative language models.
problem.friction: Open-ended generation did not provide enough structure for characters, plot choices and narrative arcs.
problem.consequence: Creators could generate text without gaining a clear way to shape or revisit the story system.
problem.statement: How might we help non-programmers direct generative storytelling through understandable narrative structures?

stages.title: Look at the creator's control problem
stages.activity: The research reviewed related authoring tools and the knowledge a creator needs to shape branching narrative.
stages.insight: The barrier was not only code; it was turning narrative concepts into editable, visible structures.
stages.decision: Make story elements manipulable instead of relying on an undirected prompt alone.

stages.title: Balance generation with authorship
stages.activity: The team framed the system around branching choices, character models, plot archetypes and narrative progression.
stages.insight: Generative assistance needed constraints that creators could understand and intentionally change.
stages.decision: Use narrative primitives as the shared language between creator and model.

stages.title: Translate theory into interface objects
stages.activity: We explored how characters, plots, attributes and branches could become visible authoring elements.
stages.insight: A structured workspace could support both AI suggestions and deliberate human editing.
stages.decision: Organize the experience around editable narrative elements and branching relationships.

stages.title: Build a creator-facing authoring environment
stages.activity: I designed and prototyped the interface that connected branching choices with AI-generated story elements.
stages.insight: The prototype made abstract narrative concepts concrete enough to inspect and discuss.
stages.decision: Keep the creator in control of structure while using the model to expand possibilities.

stages.title: Evaluate through research publication
stages.activity: The prototype and research framing were developed collaboratively for ICIDS and KIISE publication.
stages.insight: The work established a research contribution at the intersection of interaction design and generative storytelling.
stages.decision: Document the system as a research prototype rather than a finished commercial authoring product.

resolution.before: Non-programmers lacked a clear structure for directing branching stories with generative models.
resolution.response: The prototype translated characters, plots, attributes and branches into creator-facing interface elements.
resolution.after: Creators could shape generated possibilities through a visible narrative structure rather than a single open prompt.
resolution.evidence: The collaborative work produced a creator-facing research prototype and publications at ICIDS 2023 and the KIISE Conference.
resolution.reflection: Human-AI tools become more authorable when domain concepts are visible, editable and shared between person and model.

problem.context: Business-development work drew on a large professional network, current opportunities and the team's capabilities.
problem.friction: The available information did not naturally reveal which relationship deserved attention today.
problem.consequence: People could spend time reviewing connections without reaching a clear next action.
problem.statement: How might we turn a large contact network into one explainable daily business-development priority?

stages.title: Follow the daily decision
stages.activity: I reviewed how connection data, capabilities and introduction routes informed business-development choices.
stages.insight: The useful output was not another contact list; it was a reasoned next action.
stages.decision: Center the workflow on one daily target and the context needed to act.

stages.title: Bound the dashboard to a decision
stages.activity: I separated essential ranking signals from broader network information.
stages.insight: More data reduced clarity unless each signal explained why the contact mattered now.
stages.decision: Define success as a focused target with capability fit and a plausible introduction path.

stages.title: Compare feed, search and daily-priority models
stages.activity: I explored broad browsing and search before focusing the interface on a ranked daily recommendation.
stages.insight: A priority model reduced scanning while still allowing the reasoning to remain visible.
stages.decision: Lead with one target and reveal supporting signals progressively.

stages.title: Connect the recommendation to action
stages.activity: I implemented a mobile-oriented dashboard with target context, capability relevance and warm-introduction routes.
stages.insight: The recommendation became more credible when users could see why it appeared and how to proceed.
stages.decision: Pair ranking with explanation and a concrete next step.

stages.title: Refine through working-dashboard review
stages.activity: The dashboard was reviewed during the internship and documented for handoff.
stages.insight: The focused workflow clarified daily action while exposing tradeoffs in ranking and available source data.
stages.decision: Keep the interface narrow and document the assumptions behind its recommendations.

resolution.before: A large network offered many possible relationships but no clear daily priority.
resolution.response: The dashboard ranked one target and connected it to capability fit and introduction context.
resolution.after: Business-development work could begin from an explainable next action rather than an undifferentiated contact list.
resolution.evidence: A working mobile dashboard and documented internship handoff captured the end-to-end decision workflow.
resolution.reflection: Decision-support interfaces should explain why an item matters and what action follows, not only rank it.

problem.context: An industry-academia team explored how autonomous mobility could support learning experiences.
problem.friction: The concept had to communicate both a new vehicle behavior and a believable human use context.
problem.consequence: A technology-led form alone could leave the purpose and experience of the mobility system unclear.
problem.statement: How might we make an autonomous learning-mobility concept understandable through its use scenario and product expression?

stages.title: Begin with the learning scenario
stages.activity: The team used the preserved scenario and concept artifacts to frame where learning, movement and presence meet.
stages.insight: The mobility object needed to communicate a role in the experience, not only a futuristic form.
stages.decision: Anchor the concept in a recognizable learning journey.

stages.title: Connect function and meaning
stages.activity: We focused the brief on how an autonomous space could support learning while remaining legible in its environment.
stages.insight: People needed cues for both what the object does and how they relate to it.
stages.decision: Treat spatial behavior and visual identity as one design problem.

stages.title: Explore how the object signals its role
stages.activity: The team considered exterior presence, interior use and interaction cues across the journey.
stages.insight: The strongest direction made the learning purpose visible through the whole product concept.
stages.decision: Develop one coherent mobility expression instead of unrelated feature ideas.

stages.title: Make the concept visible in context
stages.activity: We developed an industry-academia design concept with product imagery and scenario-based communication.
stages.insight: Contextual visualization made the relationship between mobility and learning easier to discuss.
stages.decision: Use the artifact as a conversation prototype for the proposed experience.

stages.title: Review the concept through presentation
stages.activity: The concept was consolidated and reviewed as an industry-academia design presentation.
stages.insight: The scenario gave the product form a clearer purpose and narrative.
stages.decision: Document the result as a design concept without claiming deployment or user validation.

resolution.before: The mobility idea risked reading as technology without a clear human purpose.
resolution.response: The concept connected autonomous form, learning context and scenario communication.
resolution.after: The proposed experience could be understood as a coherent learning-mobility system.
resolution.evidence: The work was completed as a Hyundai Motor Company and Hongik University industry-academia design concept.
resolution.reflection: A future-facing product becomes more credible when its human scenario is as developed as its form.

problem.context: Job-seeking listeners were navigating podcast content inside a mobile media environment.
problem.friction: General discovery patterns did not always make professional relevance, categories or episode context easy to scan.
problem.consequence: Listeners could encounter content without quickly understanding why it fit their current goal.
problem.statement: How might we make career-oriented podcast discovery easier to scan and evaluate on mobile?

stages.title: Review the listener's discovery context
stages.activity: The industry-academia work examined preserved research boards, podcast categories and the mobile listening journey.
stages.insight: Career relevance needed to appear before a listener committed to an episode.
stages.decision: Prioritize recognizable themes, concise context and easy movement between discovery and listening.

stages.title: Reduce uncertainty before playback
stages.activity: We framed the experience around identifying relevant content and understanding an episode at a glance.
stages.insight: Discovery and episode detail were part of one decision rather than separate destinations.
stages.decision: Keep category, recommendation and episode information connected.

stages.title: Explore several paths into relevant content
stages.activity: The concept considered recent listening, category browsing, recommendation and detailed channel views.
stages.insight: Different entry points could share a consistent information hierarchy.
stages.decision: Use repeatable content patterns across the home, category and detail states.

stages.title: Build a connected mobile interface
stages.activity: The team produced interface states for discovery, categories and podcast detail within the Samsung mobile context.
stages.insight: Consistent navigation and content emphasis made the concept easier to follow across screens.
stages.decision: Carry the same listening controls and content cues through the main states.

stages.title: Review the states as one deliverable
stages.activity: The interface states and supporting research artifacts were reviewed together in the industry-academia project deliverable.
stages.insight: The connected sequence communicated the discovery concept more clearly than isolated screens.
stages.decision: Present the work as a research concept and interface proposal, without assigning a study count to this engagement.

resolution.before: Career-oriented podcast content lacked a consistently visible relevance story across discovery states.
resolution.response: The concept connected recent listening, categories, recommendations and detailed channel information.
resolution.after: Listeners could compare content and move toward playback through a clearer mobile information hierarchy.
resolution.evidence: The work produced an industry-academia research concept and a preserved set of mobile interface states.
resolution.reflection: Discovery improves when relevance is visible before commitment and remains consistent across the journey.

problem.context: A widget UX contribution had to fit an existing mobile product ecosystem during an internship.
problem.friction: The interaction needed to add useful access without competing with established navigation and visual patterns.
problem.consequence: A disconnected widget could create another surface to learn instead of making the product easier to use.
problem.statement: How might we introduce a focused widget interaction while respecting an existing mobile system?

stages.title: Read the existing system first
stages.activity: I reviewed the preserved product and widget artifacts within the scope of my UX internship contribution.
stages.insight: The design had to feel native to an established ecosystem rather than behave like a standalone feature.
stages.decision: Use existing patterns and constraints as the starting point.

stages.title: Keep the contribution bounded
stages.activity: I framed the work around the specific information and action the widget needed to expose.
stages.insight: A narrow widget purpose reduced conflict with the broader application flow.
stages.decision: Prioritize one focused interaction over feature density.

stages.title: Explore states within the host product
stages.activity: The contribution considered placement, content emphasis and transitions between widget and application contexts.
stages.insight: Continuity mattered more than giving the widget a separate visual identity.
stages.decision: Align hierarchy and behavior with the surrounding mobile system.

stages.title: Express the interaction across key states
stages.activity: I contributed widget UX screens that documented the focused interaction within the existing ecosystem.
stages.insight: Showing connected states made the intended behavior clearer than a single static layout.
stages.decision: Use a compact state sequence to communicate the contribution.

stages.title: Prepare the design for internal handoff
stages.activity: The preserved screens represent the internship design contribution prepared for team review and handoff.
stages.insight: A concise, system-aware proposal was appropriate to the ownership and scope of the work.
stages.decision: Present the project as an internship contribution without inventing independent research or product outcomes.

resolution.before: The widget needed to add utility without feeling separate from the established mobile product.
resolution.response: The UX direction used a focused interaction and system-consistent states.
resolution.after: The contribution communicated how the widget could fit the host experience without unnecessary feature depth.
resolution.evidence: The preserved interface states document the UX contribution completed during the Cheil Worldwide internship.
resolution.reflection: In a mature system, good design often means narrowing the idea until it belongs.

featured.title: UX for AI-assisted production
featured.introLead: I designed an internal tool around the problems Bubba's editors faced while preparing videos for production.
featured.introSupport: The workspace replaced scattered, manual setup with one inspectable workflow, then scaled from a 10-video prototype to more than 300 videos per automated batch.
featured.summary: An internal tool for Bubba's editors that unified scattered video-preparation tasks and scaled from a 10-video prototype to 300+ videos per automated batch.
featured.contribution: I designed and scaled the internal editor workspace, centralizing media setup, real-time monitoring, review and control in one production interface.
featured.outcome: The tool was adopted for internal production use, replacing the editors' manual clip-by-clip organization with automated batch preparation.

sections.title: Internal editors were assembling each run by hand
sections.lead: Rough-cut preparation required editors to gather footage, scripts, storyboards, voice-over files and production notes from separate sources.
sections.body: Repeating that setup clip by clip took time away from editing and became harder to track as batches grew. The internal tool needed to preserve the relationship between each input while reducing manual preparation.

featured.title: Spatial UX for collaborative design reviews
featured.introLead: A shared vehicle review needed interaction tools that could live inside the spatial scene.
featured.introSupport: The sprint translated NVIDIA Omniverse and visionOS constraints into testable annotation, part-control, presence and collaboration patterns for Apple Vision Pro.
featured.summary: A spatial design-review sprint that turned NVIDIA Omniverse and visionOS constraints into testable annotation, part-control, presence and collaboration patterns for Apple Vision Pro.
featured.contribution: On an eight-person sprint and two-person design team, I led the review-interface direction: organizing notes, measurement, part inspection and annotation history into a spatial toolbar, while collaborating with teammates who built and tested the underlying visionOS and Omniverse prototypes.
featured.outcome: The team documented where the Omniverse and visionOS collaboration models broke down, demonstrated working review interactions and shared a clear set of platform directions with Honda R&D.
featured.imageAlt: Honda spatial review slide showing Muse Pen annotation and haptic feedback interactions around a vehicle model
featured.visualCaption: Spatial annotation and haptic feedback concepts for reviewing the vehicle model.

sections.title: A shared model did not create a shared review
sections.lead: The Honda Product Visualization Sprint asked how automotive teams could review one vehicle model together in Apple Vision Pro.
sections.body: Reviewers needed to discuss details, point, measure and annotate without dropping into a detached desktop workflow or losing the physical context of the vehicle.

sections.title: Four gaps made ordinary review actions difficult
sections.body: Before designing controls, the team mapped the behaviors the streamed Omniverse experience did not support natively. Text remained screen-bound, interaction depended on custom scripts, no spatial keyboard was available and interface controls lived in extensions outside the scene.

details.label: Screen-bound text
details.body: Notes could not stay attached to the part under discussion.

details.label: Scripted actions
details.body: Basic object behaviors had to be added one at a time.

details.label: Missing input
details.body: Reviewers had no native 3D text-entry path inside Omniverse.

details.label: Detached interface
details.body: Controls lived outside the vehicle context reviewers were evaluating.

sections.title: The collaboration model conflicted at the space level
sections.body: CloudXR required a Full Immersive Space to stream the Omniverse scene, while GroupActivities and Spatial Personas operated in a Shared Space. Because only one application can own the full visual field at a time, the desired combination of a streamed vehicle and native multi-user presence could not coexist as planned.

comparison.observation: The target experience combined a streamed Omniverse model with visible remote collaborators.
comparison.response: The team built a separate spatial analogue to test the collaboration behavior and documented the platform conflict instead of hiding it.

sections.title: Native windows restored a basic review behavior
sections.body: A SwiftUI companion layer used multiple WindowGroup scenes to create independent sticky notes in visionOS Shared Space. Reviewers could use the native keyboard and place persistent windows near vehicle parts, allowing the notes to coexist visually with CloudXR even though they were not part of the Omniverse scene graph.

comparison.observation: Review notes needed spatial position and reliable text input, neither of which Omniverse supplied in the headset.
comparison.response: Treat each note as a movable native visionOS window and use visual proximity, rather than scene-graph attachment, as the bridge.

sections.title: A local bridge made vehicle parts respond
sections.body: To test direct part control without NVIDIA cloud infrastructure, the prototype connected a visionOS control to a local HTTP server and an Omniverse file watcher. A tap on the headset wrote an event that toggled a vehicle part in the live scene. The bridge was intentionally small, but the same pattern could extend to material swaps, exploded views and annotations.

flow.label: Prototype bridge

steps.label: Tap control
steps.detail: The reviewer selects a vehicle action in visionOS.

steps.label: Local request
steps.detail: A lightweight HTTP server records the requested state.

steps.label: File watcher
steps.detail: Omniverse detects the event without requiring the unavailable Channel API.

steps.detail: The selected vehicle part changes in the live model.

sections.title: Three presence models exposed different tradeoffs
sections.body: Sitting inside a virtual vehicle can hide the reviewer's real lower body, weakening orientation and comfort. The sprint compared three ways to reintroduce presence, from a static passthrough snapshot to a tracked avatar and a lighter information panel.

details.label: PeekABoo
details.body: A pre-captured lower-body image offered a simple reference but could not update in real time because third-party camera access was unavailable.

details.label: Tracked avatar
details.body: A Mixamo USDZ avatar mapped ARKit hand and world tracking into RealityKit joint transforms.

details.label: Information panel
details.body: A compact spatial panel preserved orientation with less visual and technical overhead.

sections.title: The interface brought review tools back to the vehicle
sections.body: I led the compact toolbar and review-panel direction, bringing sticky notes, Muse Pen markups, measurements, part inspection, haptic feedback, participant controls, voice annotations and annotation history into one in-session toolkit. The hierarchy kept the vehicle primary while making each review action reachable near the work.

sections.title: The prototype clarified what the platform needs next
sections.body: The demonstration gave Honda R&D both working interaction examples and a clearer system boundary. The final recommendations separated near-term infrastructure, a native Apple-platform path and a lighter-weight alternative for rendering shared 3D content.

details.label: Innoactive Hub
details.body: Test enterprise streaming infrastructure that can support the missing collaboration layer.

details.label: Native visionOS
details.body: Evaluate whether native rendering can provide sufficient visual quality with fewer space conflicts.

details.label: Gaussian splats
details.body: Explore a different representation when streamed scene complexity is the dominant constraint.

featured.title: Designing a clearer wound assessment workflow
featured.introLead: A clinical taxonomy had to become a clear, reviewable assessment workflow.
featured.introSupport: The prototype keeps wound imagery, DISH categories and terminology decisions visible throughout assessment training.
featured.summary: A clinician-facing prototype that structures how teams review wound imagery, work with DISH categories and explain terminology decisions during assessment training.
featured.contribution: I designed key interaction and interface states across guided training, keyword selection, rationale capture and assessment review within a nine-person cross-functional team, incorporating input from clinicians and industry researchers.
featured.outcome: The collaboration produced a clinician-facing prototype that keeps assessment decisions and supporting context reviewable. This work is presented as design exploration, not as a clinically validated or deployed system.
featured.imageAlt: Johnson & Johnson MedTech post-operative care and wound assessment interface concepts
featured.visualCaption: Patient and clinician interface explorations created for the Johnson & Johnson MedTech industry collaboration.

sections.title: Clinical terminology was separated from the decision
sections.body: A structured wound-assessment task can become difficult to interpret when its category, terminology and evidence are shown out of context. The training experience needed to make each decision understandable while keeping the DISH category, proposed terminology, question and progress visible.

comparison.observation: A category label or keyword alone does not explain what the reviewer is being asked to judge.
comparison.response: Frame one explicit decision at a time and keep its category and terminology in view.

sections.title: Move from validation to active classification
sections.lead: The interface evolved from confirming whether a proposed keyword matched a category to asking clinicians to choose a primary keyword and optional secondary terms alongside the wound image.
sections.body: The later flow makes the classification action more direct while retaining a visible assessment sequence.

comparison.observation: A binary confirmation can validate a suggestion, but it does not capture the clinician's own terminology choice.
comparison.response: Pair the wound evidence with primary and secondary keyword controls so classification happens in context.

sections.title: Capture disagreement,
sections.titleAccent: not just a yes or no
sections.body: When a reviewer marks a proposed keyword as irrelevant, the flow asks why. A focused feedback state preserves the category and keyword, provides space for observations and still allows the reviewer to skip when no additional context is available.

comparison.observation: A negative response identifies disagreement but leaves the reason invisible to the team reviewing the assessment.
comparison.response: Follow the decision with an optional rationale prompt tied to the exact category and keyword.

sections.title: Make the completed assessment traceable
sections.body: The review state brings the wound image, DISH category, selected keyword, clinical elements, EHR elements, additional context and image description into one record. Reviewers can move across the twelve assessments, edit a response or continue with the full decision context intact.

comparison.observation: Assessment inputs become difficult to verify when the image, terminology and supporting details are scattered across separate steps.
comparison.response: Reassemble the evidence and decisions in a single review view before the workflow continues.

facts.label: Assessments shown in the review flow

additional.title: HAiLY
additional.introLead: A long missed-charge handoff became a two-sided healthcare workflow proposal.
additional.introSupport: The concept detects incomplete encounters, routes one clear physician decision and returns traceable context to billing administrators.
additional.summary: A two-sided service concept that detects missed hospital charges, routes one clear decision to a physician and gives billing administrators a traceable follow-up workflow.
additional.contribution: I translated clinical billing-workflow research into the product architecture, administrator and physician journeys, interface direction, brand and pitch. Selected presentation slides show the product logic and interface direction while omitting pilot-result and commercial-detail pages.
additional.outcome: HAiLY earned second place at USC & Techstars Startup Weekend as a research-informed product and business concept. It remained a hackathon proposal, not a deployed clinical system.
additional.imageAlt: HAiLY presentation slide showing the administrator and physician product surfaces
additional.visualCaption: Selected HAiLY pitch-deck slide showing the two-sided product concept.

sections.title: Missed charges begin as unfinished clinical work
sections.body: A hospital encounter can remain pending when documentation and billing codes do not line up before submission. The research reframed a missed charge as a coordination problem: the administrator can see that something is incomplete, but the physician holds the context needed to resolve it.

sections.title: One unresolved encounter creates a long manual loop
sections.body: The current-state workflow required an administrator to open the EHR, filter by specialty and physician, identify a pending encounter, trace its financial and visit details, select a reason and assemble a reminder. The same case often required three to four follow-ups before a code could be confirmed or the encounter could be closed.

flow.label: Current-state follow-up

steps.label: Find
steps.detail: Filter pending encounters and locate the physician responsible for the visit.

steps.label: Trace
steps.detail: Cross-check encounter, service-date and billing context across records.

steps.label: Explain
steps.detail: Choose the missing-charge reason and prepare a physician-facing reminder.

steps.label: Repeat
steps.detail: Monitor the response, verify the correction and follow up again when needed.

flow.caption: Privacy-safe reconstruction of the researched workflow; no patient or hospital data is shown.

sections.title: The product sits between
sections.lead: HAiLY was designed as a coordination layer, not a replacement EHR.
sections.body: The agent audits incomplete encounters, packages the minimum context needed for a decision and routes a concise request to the physician before returning the validated response to the billing workflow.

comparison.observation: Administrators carried the burden of finding, explaining and repeatedly chasing each exception.
comparison.response: Detect the exception automatically, give the physician one focused validation task and preserve a visible status trail for the administrator.

sections.title: The service architecture follows the decision
sections.body: The concept connected an existing EHR or EMR to a lightweight agent layer through FHIR R4 or HL7 data ingestion. HAiLY would audit, detect and route an exception; the physician would validate the suggested action; and the confirmed information would return to billing for submission.

flow.label: Proposed service flow

steps.label: Ingest
steps.detail: Receive encounter context from systems such as Epic, Cerner or Athena through FHIR R4 or HL7.

steps.label: Audit
steps.detail: Identify a likely missed charge and assemble the relevant context.

steps.label: Validate
steps.detail: Ask the physician for a focused, one-click decision with a path to review details.

steps.label: Submit
steps.detail: Return the confirmed action to the billing workflow and update its status.

flow.caption: Conceptual architecture reconstructed from the hackathon pitch; integration was not deployed.

sections.title: Each role sees only the work it can resolve
sections.body: The product split into a desktop administrator view for oversight and a mobile physician view for decisions. The administrator needed queue health, ownership, status and escalation context; the physician needed a short explanation, the relevant encounter context and an unambiguous action.

details.label: Administrator
details.body: Scan open cases, see who owns each one, understand why it was flagged and track follow-up state.

details.label: Physician
details.body: Review one exception at a time, confirm or correct it and move on without navigating the full billing system.

sections.title: The roadmap moved from recovery to prevention
sections.body: The pitch separated the opportunity into three product phases so the concept did not depend on solving every clinical workflow at once. Each phase expanded the role of the agent while keeping a human validation point in the loop.

details.label: Retrospective recovery
details.body: Find missed charges after documentation and return them to the correct reviewer.

details.label: Real-time prevention
details.body: Surface likely omissions closer to the moment of documentation.

details.label: Continuous intelligence
details.body: Use patterns across resolved exceptions to improve routing and operational visibility.

sections.title: A complex workflow became a concise product story
sections.body: For the final pitch, I connected the operational pain point, two-sided experience, service architecture, product phases and business framing into one narrative. HAiLY placed second at USC & Techstars Startup Weekend. The award is the documented outcome; the product remains an exploratory concept rather than a validated performance claim.

sections.title: Starting with the preparedness gap
sections.body: The team used a short USC student survey and secondary research to understand awareness of anaphylaxis and emergency medication. The work pointed to a connected problem: students needed to know what to do, where treatment was available and how to reach it quickly.

sections.title: Building a campus response,
sections.body: The service proposal paired resident-assistant and public-safety training with high-risk campus locations, health partners and awareness events. Placing neffy near existing emergency infrastructure created a recognizable access model while distributing responsibility across campus teams.

sections.title: Making the nearest kit visible and actionable
sections.body: The interface concept helped a bystander locate the nearest neffy kit, check whether it was available and receive walking directions. It was framed as an integration with existing USC maps and safety or health services, not as a disconnected standalone app.

sections.title: Redesigning the case for one-handed access
sections.lead: The existing zip case requires two hands, which conflicts with the urgency and simplicity of nasal administration.
sections.body: The selected concept replaced the zipper with a single-thumb slide mechanism, kept two doses immediately available and added concise instructions, a video QR code and low-light identification.

sections.title: Extending preparedness beyond the emergency
sections.body: A friendly guardian character and campus activation concepts made education less clinical and more memorable. Scenario cards, demonstrations and portable brand touchpoints were designed to help students encounter and rehearse the response before an emergency occurs.
